brief.head: The moving bottleneck
brief.text: On a long climb, Ajay Shah said, the body com­plains about what­ever is scarcest: plenty of oxy­gen and the thighs whine; strong legs and the lungs do. {035-C03}

brief.head: Teammates, not staff
brief.text: Treat the moun­tain crew as team­mates, not hotel staff, Shah said. If they run out of creamer, take the black cof­fee, and do it with a smile. {035-C10}

brief.head: Mind the dinner
brief.text: Hiking with a CGM, Shah found that Maggi, white rice and maida still spike blood sugar. Dinner mat­ters most, he said, be­cause af­ter­wards you’re not burn­ing. {035-C13}

brief.head: Physicists on foot
brief.text: Lots of physics peo­ple go hik­ing, Shah noted, a “funny cor­re­la­tion”: you ex­pe­ri­ence grav­ity, light and air at a dif­fer­ent level al­to­gether. {#physics}

brief.head: Every fall a story
brief.text: Setbacks on the trail be­come good sto­ries later, Shah said. Amit Varma recog­nised the YouTuber’s logic: “So what if I broke my ankle? Content mila.” {035-J11}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah, in a cast, on a lifelong love of the hills
lead.head: Broken ankle, unbroken love

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 35

body: Amit Varma opened with a truth uni­ver­sally ac­knowl­edged: that which we love the most hurts us the most. His fel­low cast mem­ber, he noted, was in a cast. {035-J01}

Ajay Shah had bro­ken his ankle on a trek in the Sahyadris, his first ac­ci­dent in 45 years of hik­ing. He asked to save the story for the end, so he could place it within “some big­ger prin­ci­ples”.
The hour that fol­lowed laid out those prin­ci­ples: why go into the moun­tains, how to start, how to be­have there and when to turn back.
## Built for trees
Shah grew up on the books of Jim Corbett and on ac­counts of the first as­cent of Everest. Mountains and forests, he said, al­ways seemed like “the great­est thing in the world”.
His case for them be­gins in bi­ol­ogy. “As every good bi­ol­o­gist will say to you, we are not like mon­keys. We are mon­keys,” he said. {035-C01}

A life spent among con­crete struc­tures, cof­fee shops and bars, he ar­gued, leaves “a hole in your heart”. Varma put the same thought in a phrase from the poet Dilip Chitre: “man’s es­trange­ment from a man-made world”.

The other rea­sons came read­ily: un­plug­ging from email and phones, a beauty no pho­to­graph can con­vey, and the dis­ci­pline of putting one foot in front of the other for thou­sands of calo­ries a day.
That is done, Shah said, in a med­i­ta­tive zone where you watch your own breath­ing, heart and calves. The fit­ness needed is mod­est; the real de­mand is in the mind.
## Love, then the racket

The hosts kept re­turn­ing to what hap­pens when a pas­time be­comes a per­for­mance. Varma told of pedes­tri­an­ism, com­pet­i­tive walk­ing, which he said was America’s big­gest spec­ta­tor sport for twenty years be­fore it be­came a con­test to stay awake.
Shah summed it up: “It is the fate of every great idea to start out as a move­ment and then be­come a busi­ness and then be­come a racket.”
Varma’s an­ti­dote came from the chess grand­mas­ter Tigran Petrosian, who, asked whether he was play­ing to win or to draw, said he was “play­ing to play”.

Shah had made the same point ear­lier about the hard­est call in the moun­tains, when to turn back. Years of train­ing are a sunk cost, and a sum­mit photo for Facebook is no rea­son to go on. “Life is not lived as a per­for­mance to show other peo­ple,” he said. {035-C04}
## Never relax
On the trail, he asked for man­ners: no lit­ter, no Bluetooth speak­ers, and talk in hushed whis­pers, so the birds come closer.

Then came the ankle. After a long day’s climb up Tung, Shah re­laxed at a chai shop over fresh lime soda, not know­ing that 300 me­tres of de­scent still lay be­tween him and the lake where they would camp. In fail­ing light, his group fol­lowed a pipe down­hill, and he fell.
“You can never let your guard down,” he said. “You have to be there with full pres­ence and en­ergy.” {035-C12}
Varma re­called Tom Vanderbilt’s *Traffic*, which found that most ac­ci­dents hap­pen close to home, when the brain switches off.
Asked how hik­ing had shaped him, Shah said he could not imag­ine him­self with­out it. “If I had not been an econ­o­mist, I would be a bi­ol­o­gist.” {035-J18}

second.label: A chess parable
second.head: Neither win nor draw
second.deck: A chess story Amit Varma offers as everybody’s philosophy for life

pic.caption: Tigran Petrosian at the chess tournament in Beverwijk in 1960

body: An op­po­nent who badly wanted a draw once leaned for­ward to test the wa­ters with Tigran Petrosian, the great grand­mas­ter and pi­o­neer of the ex­change sac­ri­fice. Was he play­ing to win? No. To draw? No. Then why was he play­ing? {035-S05}
“I’m play­ing to play,” Petrosian said. Amit Varma, who told the story, wanted it adopted as a creed: “I’m hik­ing to hike. I’m walk­ing to walk. Nothing else kind of mat­ters.”

Ajay Shah said com­pe­ti­tion had never crept into his own moun­tain life, and called rock-climbing races “non­sense”. Climbing is meant to be an iso­lated, as­cetic project in which you solve a moun­tain, he said, like a cross­word. {#crossword}

quote.text: This should be everybody’s phi­los­o­phy for life, that it is not about the win, it is not about the re­sult.

third.head: Old legs, young laggards

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Bangalore teenagers

body: Ajay Shah and his friend KP Krishnan once went hik­ing to Panchachuli, near the India-China bor­der in Uttarakhand. Their com­pan­ions were a band of teenage boys and girls from Bangalore.

The two older men as­sumed they would be the weak­est link of the chain. Instead they were among the strong­est. The teenagers’ lack of fit­ness, Shah said, was out­ra­geous: their lives were spent sit­ting on their butts with video games and Netflix.
“It is re­ally a new rev­e­la­tion for me,” he said. “The idea that you can be young and not phys­i­cally ac­tive.” {035-S07}

The story was Shah’s an­swer to Amit Varma, who had taken an ear­lier jibe about Netflix per­son­ally. “My ques­tion for you is on whose butt should I sit,” Varma had asked. “I’ll sit on my butt only, no?” {035-J08}

p2.title: Why we walk
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s case for the mountains, from a childhood of Jim Corbett to a cast, as questioned by Amit Varma

quote.text: I’ve been going out into the moun­tains from age 13 and I’ve just con­sis­tently gone back.

box.title: The books that started it
box.text: Ajay Shah grew up on Jim Corbett’s books and on ac­counts of the first as­cent of Everest. He rec­om­mends three Corbett books in se­quence: *Man-eaters of Kumaon*, *The Man-eating Leopard of Rudraprayag* and *Jungle Lore*. “Everybody will enjoy them,” he says. {035-R01}

sections.label: The first love
sections.head: A boy, a book and a mountain
sections.caption: a lifelong love of the hills
body: Ajay Shah has been going into the moun­tains since he was 13, and never stopped. Many peo­ple, he said, give up in their teens and twen­ties. “I just kept going.” {035-S01}
Reading planted the seed. Move *For Whom the Bell Tolls*, one of the great books of the world, to a purely urban set­ting, Shah said, and “the oomph is lost”. {035-R06}

At IIT Bombay in the early 1980s he found a com­mu­nity ready-made. A physics pro­fes­sor, Professor Mahajan, had led the build­ing of a moun­taineer­ing cul­ture there. Gear was scarce, so it was pooled, and know-how was handed down. Today, Shah said, the in­ter­net, GPS and cheap gear do that job.
## The hole in the heart
Amit Varma asked whether em­brac­ing na­ture makes you a dif­fer­ent per­son, bor­row­ing Dilip Chitre’s phrase “man’s es­trange­ment from a man-made world”. {035-R09}
Shah said yes. Modern think­ing, he said, has stretched Karl Marx’s idea of alien­ation be­yond the as­sem­bly-line worker: we are mon­keys, meant to live among trees. {035-C01}

When Varma, look­ing at each cam­era in turn, warned that the hosts were not fans of Marx, Shah dis­agreed slightly. Marx, he said, was first to see how the mar­ket econ­omy is a “wild west wind” that tears down feu­dal­ism. {035-C02}
~ He was wrong, Shah added, on es­sen­tially every rem­edy. Varma replied that get­ting the de­scrip­tion right and the pre­scrip­tion wrong is prac­ti­cally part of left­ism.

quote.text: I’ve been going out into the moun­tains from age 13 and I’ve just con­sis­tently gone back.

portraits.caption: Karl Marx
portraits.credit: John Jabez Edwin Mayall, public domain

sections.label: The why
sections.head: Hiking to hike
sections.caption: why anyone climbs
body: Amit Varma had long been fas­ci­nated by the bod­ies pre­served on Everest, among them the one in the fa­mous Green Boots pho­to­graph. Why, he asked, do peo­ple climb at all? {#greenboots}

Ajay Shah said he could give lots of ex post rea­son­ing, and “maybe it is all con­trived”. As a child he sim­ply had to go out into forests and moun­tains. Being away from email and phones, he said, calms the mind and makes you think.
There is beauty: the sun­rise at Panchachuli, the paw­prints of snow leop­ards. A keen pho­tog­ra­pher, he said noth­ing can re­pro­duce the 3D sen­sa­tion of being there. {#photo}
## The mind you carry
There is also the phys­i­cal dis­ci­pline of walk­ing for hours in a med­i­ta­tive zone. His friend KP Krishnan re­cites thou­sands of Sanskrit shlokas as he goes.
Perhaps, Shah said, *Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance* has it right: the Zen you find in the moun­tain is the Zen that you take up there. {035-R10}
~ What spoils it is per­for­mance. Competition had never crept into his own life with the forests and moun­tains, Shah said; for him it has been “a zone of pu­rity”.

quote.text: The Zen you find in the moun­tain is the Zen that you take up there.
quote.who: Robert M. Pirsig, as quoted by Ajay Shah

sections.label: The how
sections.head: First a day, then forever
sections.caption: the first day hike
body: “We said to gen­tle reader, get off your butt and read some books,” Ajay Shah said. “Today we’re say­ing, gen­tle reader, get off your butt and go take a hike.” {035-J05}
Everyone should start with a day hike, he said: a small back­pack, two litres of water, five ap­ples and a route, ide­ally with peo­ple who know it. {#dayhike}

If you reach a sum­mit wish­ing you did not have to go back the same day, some­thing is turn­ing in­side your heart. Pitch a tent. Then two nights, seven, ten. In mod­ern India, he said, tents beat the caves and tem­ples where hik­ers once slept.
On a north-south route in Maharashtra, he and Ayush Patnaik have looked at each other around day seven and re­alised they could keep going till Kanyakumari. {035-C08}
## Not a high ask

The fit­ness needed is mod­est. A day may burn two, three or four thou­sand calo­ries, but in stints of up to an hour on gen­tle slopes, with breaks. If you can row or run for 10 to 20 min­utes, you are ready. The de­mand, Shah said, is in the mind. {035-C06}
~ Loads are an­other mat­ter. In the Himalayas, porters, mules or the zo, a yak-cow cross, carry them. In Maharashtra you carry your own, be­tween 5 and 15 per cent of body weight. {#load}

quote.text: The de­mand is in the mind, mean­ing it’s about the mind being able to han­dle the body.

sections.label: Dos and don’ts
sections.head: Whisper, and the birds come
sections.caption: manners in the mountains
body: Ajay Shah’s first rule was to come pre­pared. On easy routes like Triund be­hind Dharamshala, and on pil­grim­ages to Gangotri, he has seen peo­ple in party clothes in ab­ject mis­ery, in­spired by mirac­u­lous things seen on YouTube.

Their grand­par­ents were agri­cul­tural work­ers, with the strength that comes from that. “But in today’s world, if you’re sit­ting on your butt watch­ing Netflix and eat­ing pro­cessed food, you’re not ready,” he said. {035-C07}

Then he pleaded. Do not lit­ter: there is no­body to clean up. Do not play music, which car­ries for hun­dreds of me­tres in the si­lence. Speak in whis­pers, and the birds and wildlife will come to you. {035-C09}
Wet wipes should be all cot­ton, he added. Nylon and polyester are plas­tics, and would pol­lute the moun­tains for a thou­sand years.
## Teammates
The crew car­ries your load and cooks and washes up at al­ti­tude. Treat them as team­mates, Shah said, and take no for an an­swer with a smile, even when the creamer runs out. {035-C10}
Amit Varma ob­served that the ad­vice is needed only be­cause “we are dis­gust­ing in our ev­ery­day lives”.
~ When things go wrong, Shah stays calm. Once, atop Harishchandragad, Arul Menezes began howl­ing with kid­ney stones. “Have you asked Arul be­fore shar­ing this anec­dote?” Varma asked. {035-J10}

quote.text: Treat them like team­mates, don’t treat them like your em­ploy­ees.

sections.label: The recco
sections.head: Kit and caboodle
sections.caption: kit, books and water filters
body: Ajay Shah’s books were three by Jim Corbett and two by Jon Krakauer, *Into Thin Air* and *Into the Wild*. Then came the kit.
After a life­time of hunt­ing for the right equip­ment, he called the ar­rival of Decathlon a break­through: good gear, read­ily avail­able and af­ford­able. {#decathlon}
A day hike needs only the back­pack lying around your house. For big trips he ad­vises 75 litres, enough for a sleep­ing bag and clothes; peo­ple often buy too small or too big. {#pack}
He strongly en­cour­aged women to hike, for the free­dom it brings and the abil­ity to deal with ad­ver­sity, not­ing only that women’s back­packs are cut dif­fer­ently.

For water, he loves the LifeStraw bot­tle: fill it with bad water, suck, and what comes out is cleaner than any tap water in India. {#lifestraw} For plan­ning, he starts with the Indiahikes web­site and moves to the desk­top ver­sion of Google Earth.
## The tech­nol­ogy of walk­ing
Amit Varma brought an essay by Adam Gopnik, who writes that our backs and arches, “like queru­lous cab­i­net min­is­ters, at first com­plain and then re­sign”. {#gopnik}
~ Walking for plea­sure, Gopnik ar­gues, has de­pended on tech­nol­ogy: gaslight in London, the rule of law, and from the 1980s the Walkman and cush­ioned sneak­ers. {035-C14}

quote.text: It is some­thing that is far eas­ier for us to do in mod­ern times
So once you get going, it’s re­ally un­stop­pable and you don’t feel like stop­ping. You don’t feel like com­ing back. You can just keep on going for­ever.

p3.title: Tales from the trail
p3.deck: A fall, a freezing night, a porter’s ferries and a lost bet on Lincoln

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Tung, a pipe and a broken ankle
stories.head: A lime soda before the fall
body: In the Sahyadris there is a moun­tain top called Tung. Look north from it, Ajay Shah said, and there is a lake. That lake­side was where his group meant to pitch their tents.

Tung was their sec­ond up-and-down climb of the day. From the top they could see the camp­site. Shah began to relax: they had done about a thou­sand me­tres up and five hun­dred down, and now, he thought, it got eas­ier. {#thousandup}
Back at the base there was a chai shop. They daw­dled over fresh lime soda while the sun went down, think­ing only a kilo­me­tre or two of flat walk­ing re­mained.

They were wrong. Had he looked up the el­e­va­tions of the sum­mit, the base and the lake on Google Earth, Shah said, he would have known there were still 300 me­tres of de­scent to go. {#descent} From the top of Tung, which he put at about 1,100 me­tres, the view had flat­tened the ter­rain. {#tung}

They set off late in fail­ing light and got a lit­tle lost. A pipe led down to the lake, so they fol­lowed it. That was an el­e­men­tary error, Shah said: peo­ple build pipes along the short­est line, which is also the steep­est.
Then came the dumb luck. He fell, and broke his ankle: his first ac­ci­dent in 45 years of hik­ing.

~ The fall it­self was luck, he said, but lazi­ness about home­work and a low­ered guard had made the con­di­tions for it. His notes to self: “Do a lit­tle more home­work.” And: “Never relax until the tent is up.” {035-S06}
stories.why: Danger peaks when the job feels done. From above, Amit Varma said, the last stretch of a book or an ar­ti­cle al­ways seems flat. And Tom Vanderbilt’s *Traffic* found that most ac­ci­dents hap­pen close to home. {035-R12}
stories.postscript: Of the cast it­self, Shah had no good word: “The cast has no re­deem­ing fea­tures.” {#cast}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the fall below Tung

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah at Goechala, and the call to turn back
stories.head: Cold fingers, warm regrets
body: On the Goechala trek, the Sikkim-side ap­proach to Kanchenjunga, Ajay Shah spent the night at the last camp­site, Lamuney, per­haps 4,500 or 4,800 me­tres up. {#lamuney} The wind came up. In merino, fleece and a jacket, in­side a sleep­ing bag, he could not sleep for the cold.
At 4 a.m. they set off in ghostly moon­light, two or three breaths to every step. They reached Goechala 1, with Kanchenjunga be­fore them.
His guide said he could make Goechala 2. Shah said no: his gloves were bad, his fin­ger­tips hurt, and it was per­haps minus 10, or minus 20. {#minus}
~ He still wishes he had gone on. “All I know is that at that mo­ment I des­per­ately wanted to go,” he said, “but I made the call that I can’t han­dle this, I’m going back.” {035-S02}
stories.why: The hard­est call in the moun­tains is when to stop. Every ac­ci­dent on Everest, Shah said, comes down to that judg­ment, and Jon Krakauer’s *Into Thin Air* shows it on the final sum­mit day. {035-R04}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma, who wor­ries about friends who take risks, was re­lieved. “You still have your fin­gers,” he said.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the cold night at Lamuney

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s third year at IIT Bombay, as a porter
stories.head: The coolie who came down first
body: The west face of Harishchandragad, Ajay Shah said, is worse than ver­ti­cal: Konkan Kada, a cobra-shaped over­hang that looks down into the Konkan and al­most to the sea.

In his third year at IIT Bombay, the in­sti­tute made its first suc­cess­ful climb of the face, and Shah was a coolie, car­ry­ing food, water and climb­ing stores. He made two end­less fer­ries up and down with 20 kg tied to his hip. {035-S03}
“I have not done much tech­ni­cal climb­ing my­self,” he said. “I was just a user of other people’s rope sys­tems.”

~ On the last day he was first out. He rap­pelled about 1,800 feet through sheer over­hang, and at each stop the rope’s nat­u­ral twist spun him through 360 de­grees, so he took pho­to­graphs all around. {#rappel}
stories.why: You need not be the star to be part of some­thing his­toric. Carrying food, water and climb­ing stores for some­one else’s climb gave Ajay Shah what he called “an­other mem­o­rable life ex­pe­ri­ence”.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on carrying loads up Konkan Kada

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Edward Weston and the six-day walkers
stories.head: Lincoln won, so Weston walked
body: Amit Varma took the story from Matthew Algeo’s *Pedestrianism*. In 1860, Edward Weston bet a friend that if Lincoln won, he would walk from the State House in Boston to the Capitol in Washington in ten days. {#weston}
Lincoln won. Weston walked, ar­rived late and missed the in­au­gu­ra­tion, but the whole coun­try fol­lowed him. Then he de­cided walk­ing should be a com­pet­i­tive sport.

For twenty years it was America’s big­gest spec­ta­tor sport. {#twenty} Crowds paid to watch men go round and round six days a week. Weston, in hunt­ing boots and breeches, was its Federer; the Irish work­ing man Dan O’Leary its Nadal; O’Leary’s protégé Frank Hart, “Black Dan”, a third pil­lar.

~ Early on, fans com­pared Weston’s long strides with O’Leary’s shorter, lighter steps. Later tech­nique stopped mat­ter­ing. “It be­comes a bat­tle of stay­ing awake,” Varma said. “They are fight­ing sleep.” {035-S04}
stories.why: Varma said an ac­tiv­ity done for love can turn com­pet­i­tive, then a spec­ta­cle, then toxic. Ajay Shah’s sum­mary: every great idea starts as a move­ment, be­comes a busi­ness, then be­comes a racket. {035-C05}
stories.postscript: Varma imag­ines the old cham­pi­ons, once the sport died, walk­ing alone again and re­dis­cov­er­ing why they loved it.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 35. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Karl Marx (John Jabez Edwin Mayall, public domain); Jim Corbett (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Tigran Petrosian (Wikimedia Commons, CC0); Ernest Hemingway (Lloyd Arnold, public domain); Jon Krakauer (Devon Christopher Adams, CC BY-SA 2.0).

shelf.title: Man-eaters of Kumaon
shelf.creator: Jim Corbett
shelf.why: Part of the read­ing that made moun­tains and forests seem like ‘the great­est thing in the world’ to him.

shelf.title: The Man-eating Leopard of Rudraprayag
shelf.creator: Jim Corbett
shelf.why: One of the three Corbett books he con­sid­ers great.

shelf.title: Jungle Lore
shelf.creator: Jim Corbett
shelf.why: Completes his rec­om­mended Corbett se­quence.

shelf.title: Into Thin Air
shelf.creator: Jon Krakauer
shelf.why: It is about one sum­mer on Everest when many bad things hap­pened, and it shows the go/no-go call on the final sum­mit day.

shelf.title: Into the Wild
shelf.creator: Jon Krakauer
shelf.why: Ajay says Krakauer has ‘some re­ally good books’ and this is an­other one.

shelf.title: For Whom the Bell Tolls
shelf.creator: Ernest Hemingway
shelf.why: He calls it one of the great books of the world.

shelf.title: Biophilia
shelf.creator: Edward O. Wilson
shelf.why: E.O.

shelf.title: Prem Throws Your Heart to the Ground
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It leads into his ques­tion of whether urban, thing-filled liv­ing es­tranges us from some­thing es­sen­tial.

shelf.title: Father Returning Home
shelf.creator: Dilip Chitre
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite poems, whose phrase ‘man’s es­trange­ment from a man-made world’ and clos­ing image of ‘no­mads en­ter­ing a sub­con­ti­nent through a nar­row pass’ have stayed with him.

shelf.title: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
shelf.creator: Robert M. Pirsig
shelf.why: Its line ‘the Zen you find in the moun­tain is the Zen that you take up there’ cap­tures his point: what you get from the moun­tains de­pends on the mind you bring.

shelf.title: Pedestrianism
shelf.creator: Matthew Algeo
shelf.why: It is a vivid case of a pas­time loved for it­self being turned into a com­pet­i­tive spec­ta­cle and turn­ing ugly.

shelf.title: Traffic
shelf.creator: Tom Vanderbilt
shelf.why: Vanderbilt doc­u­ments that a large share of ac­ci­dents hap­pen close to home, when fa­mil­iar ground makes driv­ers switch off, which is ex­actly what hap­pened to Ajay on a hike.

shelf.title: Heaven’s Gaits
shelf.creator: Adam Gopnik
shelf.why: Amit en­joys its lines (‘our backs and arches, like queru­lous cab­i­net min­is­ters, at first com­plain and then resign’).

shelf.title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s ac­count of re­vers­ing his di­a­betes through diet: eat less ce­real, avoid pro­cessed food, and treat ghee as a su­per­food and sugar as poi­son.

shelf.title: Decathlon
shelf.why: After a life­time of hunt­ing for the right equip­ment, he calls Decathlon’s ar­rival a break­through: good gear, read­ily avail­able and af­ford­able.

shelf.title: A 75-litre backpack (Ajay uses the Volt 75), and a women’s-fit pack for women
shelf.why: Any old back­pack works for a day hike.

shelf.title: LifeStraw bottle
shelf.creator: LifeStraw
shelf.why: You can fill it with any bad water, and suck­ing pushes it through a fil­ter.

shelf.title: Katadyn gravity-fed water filter
shelf.creator: Katadyn
shelf.why: You fill a six-litre bag and grav­ity pushes the water through a fil­ter.

shelf.title: Indiahikes website
shelf.creator: Indiahikes
shelf.why: Ajay has never used them as a ser­vices firm, but for al­most any hike in India their page is often the best, with the story, the route and a map.

shelf.title: Google Earth (desktop version)
shelf.creator: Google
shelf.why: Ajay’s ‘paradise’ on a big screen: ter­rain mode, 3D views and aerial fly­bys, plus a prac­ti­cal use for hik­ers, check­ing the el­e­va­tions of sum­mit, base and camp­site be­fore you go.

shelf.title: Odati
shelf.why: Ajay has gone with them on many of his trips and likes their work a lot.

shelf.title: White Magic Adventure Travel
shelf.why: It runs a fixed cal­en­dar of treks, so you can show up alone and join oth­ers with­out or­gan­is­ing your own group.

shelf.title: Gorakhgad and Kothaligad day hikes
shelf.why: They are an easy first step: a back­pack, two litres of water, five ap­ples and some route-finding.

shelf.title: Harishchandragad and Ratangad
shelf.why: He calls it world class and says he has never seen any­thing more beau­ti­ful.

shelf.title: Goechala trek
shelf.why: Of all his Himalayan treks, he rates it one of the best of his life.

laughs.text: Amit’s open­ing: ‘It is a truth uni­ver­sally ac­knowl­edged that that which we love the most hurts us the most. And today you will see my fel­low cast mem­ber in a cast.’ Then, on Ajay say­ing the worst is be­hind him: ‘though at that time I was stand­ing be­hind you.’

Amit on Ajay’s mes­sage mid-hike: Ajay had said ‘Amit, you won’t hear from me for a week’, and ‘in the mid­dle of that bliss­ful pe­riod of men­tal peace and calm’ came the news that he’d bro­ken his ankle. Amit also calls him a hik­ing evan­ge­list, mean­ing ‘a per­son who evan­ge­lises hik­ing and not that while hik­ing you evan­ge­lise.’

Amit, look­ing at each cam­era in turn, warns view­ers that Ajay’s ‘great German philosopher’ (Marx) and ‘the good Lord intended’ are ironic: ‘we are not ac­tu­ally fans of Marx... at least I am cer­tain there is no good lord. However, mon­keys do exist and we are mon­keys.’
On the back­ground music from a fes­ti­val two vil­lages away: ‘This is not green screen, though it is green... This is also a part of na­ture. Humans are mon­keys.’

Ajay’s call to ac­tion: ‘We said to gen­tle reader, get off your butt and read some books. Today we’re say­ing, gen­tle reader, get off your butt and go take a hike.’ Amit hopes lis­ten­ers are get­ting up to walk ‘not be­cause they’re sick of the show.’
After Ajay says you should be able to ‘row or run’ for 20 min­utes, Amit clar­i­fies: ‘by row we mean the English row’, a bilin­gual pun on the Hindi for cry­ing.

Told hik­ers should carry 5-15% of body weight, Amit says: ‘This is why, Ajay, you should be over­weight like me, be­cause then you’re car­ry­ing a lower per­cent­age.’ Ajay: ‘I don’t rec­om­mend it.’
Amit, stung by the Netflix jibe: ‘My ques­tion for you is on whose butt should I sit. I’ll sit on my butt only, no?’
Ajay ex­plains the zo, a yak-cow cross with ‘the strength of the yak and the do­mes­tic­ity of a cow’. Amit: ‘Jimi Hendrix has a song called Hazo. I won­der whether he was think­ing of it.’
After Ajay re­calls Arul Menezes howl­ing with kid­ney stones atop Harishchandragad, Amit asks: ‘Have you asked Arul be­fore shar­ing this anec­dote?’
Amit on turn­ing mishaps into sto­ries: ‘That is how YouTubers think of con­tent. So what if I broke my ankle? Content mila.’
On the five ap­ples for a day hike, Amit: ‘And by ap­ples you mean the fruit, not iPad and MacBook.’
Green Boots: Amit men­tions the fa­mous pho­to­graph of one of the bod­ies pre­served on Everest, which led him to ask why peo­ple climb at all.

Amit casts the pedes­tri­an­ism greats as ten­nis greats: Weston as Federer, Dan O’Leary as Nadal, and Frank ‘Black Dan’ Hart as a pos­si­ble Djokovic. He likens the na­tional frenzy over Weston’s walk to Lindbergh’s a few decades later.
Amit on France, home of Decathlon, as a great out­door-sports cul­ture and a cen­tre of ultra-running, home to the UTMB (Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc).
Ajay’s clos­ing self-portrait: ‘if I had not been an econ­o­mist, I would be a bi­ol­o­gist.’
